--- title: "Tracking Spending" engine: knitr webr: packages: - dplyr pyodide: packages: - pandas --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## How these exercises work Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. **Level 1 (Guided)** fills in the blanks of a finished function. **Level 2 (Practice)** applies it to new numbers. **Level 3 (Challenge)** asks a new question with little scaffolding. The R and Python exercises run in your browser: click **Run Code** to try, **Submit Answer** to check, and use the hint or solution if you get stuck. Excel exercises have a solution you can reveal. ::: ## Book Topics - **Tracking vs. budgeting**: tracking records where money actually went; budgeting allocates where it should go; comparing the two creates a feedback loop - **Capture methods**: spending journal, checkbook register, cash envelopes, bank statements; pick one and run it for a full month - **Categorizing**: start with about 10 stable buckets (housing, transportation, groceries, dining out, subscriptions, personal, health, gifts, fun money, other); when in doubt use "Other", and only promote a new category after seeing it three months in a row - **Using spreadsheets**: bank exports have `Date`, `Description`, and `Amount` columns; a keyword lookup adds the `Category` column in one pass - **Monthly review**: pull, categorize, compare to budget, and pick *one* change for next month - **Online subscriptions**: Americans spend about $219/month on subscriptions and underestimate it by $133; audit every quarter and cancel anything unused in 30 days - **Math**: the subscription audit, the opportunity cost of a $20/month subscription invested at 7% for 30 years (about $22,700) ## Bank Statement Data A minimal bank export has three columns: `Date`, `Description`, and `Amount`. The code blocks below show how to create an example bank statement file in R, Python, and Excel. ::: panel-tabset ## Excel We can simply copy and paste the data into Excel; `Date` in A, `Description` in B, `Amount` in C. ![`bank_statement` in Excel](img/tracking_spending-bank-statement.png){width='75%' fig-align='center'} ## Python In Python, we'll use `polars` to create a `DataFrame` and display the bank statement. This is similar to the `tibble` we created above. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import polars as pl py_bank_statement = pl.DataFrame({ "Date": [ "2026-01-02", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-06", "2026-01-07", "2026-01-08", "2026-01-09", "2026-01-10", "2026-01-11", "2026-01-12", "2026-01-13", "2026-01-14", "2026-01-15" ], "Description": [ "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness" ], "Amount": [ 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99 ] }).with_columns(pl.col("Date").str.to_date()) py_bank_statement ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r_bank_statement <- tibble::tibble( Date = as.Date(c( "2026-01-02", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-06", "2026-01-07", "2026-01-08", "2026-01-09", "2026-01-10", "2026-01-11", "2026-01-12", "2026-01-13", "2026-01-14", "2026-01-15" )), Description = c( "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness" ), Amount = c( 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99 ) ) r_bank_statement |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Date |Description | Amount| |:----------|:--------------------|--------:| |2026-01-02 |Employer Payroll | 2400.00| |2026-01-02 |Rent | -1500.00| |2026-01-03 |Comcast Internet | -75.00| |2026-01-03 |Trader Joe's | -82.45| |2026-01-04 |Shell Gas | -45.20| |2026-01-04 |Netflix | -15.99| |2026-01-05 |Starbucks | -6.75| |2026-01-06 |PG&E Electric | -142.30| |2026-01-07 |AT&T Wireless | -85.00| |2026-01-08 |Spotify | -10.99| |2026-01-09 |Whole Foods | -64.12| |2026-01-10 |Chipotle | -14.50| |2026-01-11 |Geico Auto Insurance | -125.00| |2026-01-12 |NYTimes Digital | -17.00| |2026-01-13 |Shell Gas | -42.80| |2026-01-14 |Costco | -156.78| |2026-01-15 |24 Hour Fitness | -39.99| ::: ::: We can view the bank statement in R using `knitr::kable()`. ::: ## Categorizing Transactions A bank export only says *where* the money went (`Description`). Adding a `Category` column turns a list of merchants into budget buckets. In R, `dplyr::case_when()` checks each rule in order and the first match wins; in Python, `numpy.select()` does the same with a list of conditions and a list of labels; in Excel, `IFS()` does it one cell at a time. Anything that matches no rule falls into "Other". ### Level 1: Guided Fill in the blanks so grocery stores (Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, Costco) become "Groceries" and everything without a rule becomes "Other". How many transactions are groceries? ::: panel-tabset #### Excel With `Description` in column `B`, write an `IFS()` formula in `D2` that labels subscriptions, groceries, and "Other", then fill it down and count the groceries. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution `SEARCH()` finds a keyword in a cell, `ISNUMBER()` turns that into true/false, and `OR()` joins several keywords. The final `TRUE, "Other"` catches everything else. ```swift =IFS( OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Netflix",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Spotify",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("NYTimes",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("24 Hour Fitness",B2))), "Subscriptions", OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Trader Joe",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Whole Foods",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Costco",B2))), "Groceries", TRUE, "Other" ) ``` ![`IFS()` in Excel](img/tracking_spending-ifs.png){width='100%' fig-align='center'} Then count them with `=COUNTIF(D:D, "Groceries")`. The answer is 3. ::: #### Python ::: {.cell exercise='cat_1_py' setup='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_1_py #| setup: true import numpy as np import pandas as pd statement = pd.DataFrame({ "Description": [ "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness"], "Amount": [ 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99] }) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_1_py'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_1_py desc = statement["Description"] statement["Category"] = np.select( [desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"), desc.str.contains(______)], ["Subscriptions", "Groceries"], default=______ ) (statement["Category"] == "Groceries").sum() ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="cat_1_py"} Separate the store names with `|` (it means "or"): `"Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco"`. The default label is `"Other"`. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="cat_1_py"} ```python desc = statement["Description"] statement["Category"] = np.select( [desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"), desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco")], ["Subscriptions", "Groceries"], default="Other" ) (statement["Category"] == "Groceries").sum() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_1_py' check='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_1_py #| check: true if result == 3: feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, and Costco."} else: feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. List all three stores, separated by |."} feedback ``` ::: #### R ::: {.cell exercise='cat_1_r' setup='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_1_r #| setup: true library(dplyr) statement <- data.frame( Description = c( "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness"), Amount = c( 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_1_r'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_1_r statement |> mutate(Category = case_when( grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions", grepl(______, Description) ~ "Groceries", TRUE ~ ______ )) |> filter(Category == "Groceries") |> nrow() ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="cat_1_r"} Separate the store names with `|` (it means "or"): `"Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco"`. The last rule's label is `"Other"`. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="cat_1_r"} ```r statement |> mutate(Category = case_when( grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions", grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries", TRUE ~ "Other" )) |> filter(Category == "Groceries") |> nrow() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_1_r' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_1_r #| check: true if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 3))) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, and Costco.") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. List all three stores, separated by |.") } ``` ::: ::: ### Level 2: Practice Next month's export has three new merchants: Safeway (groceries), Hulu (a subscription), and Uber (transportation). The rules below don't know them yet, so they land in "Other". Update the rules so no transaction is left in "Other". ::: panel-tabset #### Excel Your `IFS()` formula labels the new month's Safeway, Hulu, and Uber rows as "Other". Edit it so `=COUNTIF(D:D, "Other")` returns 0. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution Add each new merchant to its group with another `ISNUMBER(SEARCH(...))` inside the `OR()`, and add a Transportation rule: ```swift OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Safeway",B2))), "Groceries", OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Hulu",B2))), "Subscriptions", OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Shell",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Uber",B2))), "Transportation", ``` Re-fill the formula down after editing it. ::: #### Python ::: {.cell exercise='cat_2_py' setup='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_2_py #| setup: true import numpy as np import pandas as pd statement = pd.DataFrame({ "Description": ["Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Safeway", "Hulu", "Netflix", "Uber Trip", "Shell Gas", "Chipotle"], "Amount": [2400.00, -1500.00, -71.20, -17.99, -15.99, -23.40, -44.10, -13.25] }) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_2_py'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_2_py desc = statement["Description"] statement["Category"] = np.select( [desc.str.contains("Payroll"), desc.str.contains("Rent"), desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco"), desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"), desc.str.contains("Shell"), desc.str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")], ["Income", "Housing", "Groceries", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Dining"], default="Other" ) (statement["Category"] == "Other").sum() ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="cat_2_py"} Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by `|`. For example, `"Shell|Uber"`. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="cat_2_py"} ```python desc = statement["Description"] statement["Category"] = np.select( [desc.str.contains("Payroll"), desc.str.contains("Rent"), desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway"), desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu"), desc.str.contains("Shell|Uber"), desc.str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")], ["Income", "Housing", "Groceries", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Dining"], default="Other" ) (statement["Category"] == "Other").sum() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_2_py' check='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_2_py #| check: true if result == 0: feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: every transaction has a home."} else: feedback = {"correct": False, "message": f"{result} transaction(s) are still 'Other'. Check Safeway, Hulu, and Uber."} feedback ``` ::: #### R ::: {.cell exercise='cat_2_r' setup='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_2_r #| setup: true library(dplyr) statement <- data.frame( Description = c("Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Safeway", "Hulu", "Netflix", "Uber Trip", "Shell Gas", "Chipotle"), Amount = c(2400.00, -1500.00, -71.20, -17.99, -15.99, -23.40, -44.10, -13.25) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_2_r'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_2_r statement |> mutate(Category = case_when( grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income", grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing", grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries", grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions", grepl("Shell", Description) ~ "Transportation", grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining", TRUE ~ "Other" )) |> filter(Category == "Other") |> nrow() ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="cat_2_r"} Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by `|`. For example, `"Shell|Uber"`. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="cat_2_r"} ```r statement |> mutate(Category = case_when( grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income", grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing", grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway", Description) ~ "Groceries", grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu", Description) ~ "Subscriptions", grepl("Shell|Uber", Description) ~ "Transportation", grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining", TRUE ~ "Other" )) |> filter(Category == "Other") |> nrow() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_2_r' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_2_r #| check: true if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0))) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: every transaction has a home.") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = paste(.result, "transaction(s) are still 'Other'. Check Safeway, Hulu, and Uber.")) } ``` ::: ::: ### Level 3: Challenge Real bank exports are messy: the same merchant can show up as `NETFLIX.COM`, `Netflix`, or `netflix`. The rule below only matches the exact capitalization, so it finds just 1 of the 3 subscriptions. Change the code so capitalization doesn't matter, and count the subscriptions again. ::: panel-tabset #### Excel Does the `IFS()` and `SEARCH()` formula need any change for `NETFLIX.COM`? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution No. `SEARCH()` ignores capitalization, so `SEARCH("Netflix", "NETFLIX.COM")` already finds a match. (Its case-sensitive cousin is `FIND()`.) ::: #### Python ::: {.cell exercise='cat_3_py' setup='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_3_py #| setup: true import pandas as pd messy = pd.DataFrame({ "Description": ["NETFLIX.COM", "Spotify USA", "nytimes digital", "SHELL OIL 1234", "Whole Foods #102"], "Amount": [-15.99, -10.99, -17.00, -45.20, -64.12] }) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_3_py'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_3_py is_sub = messy["Description"].str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness") is_sub.sum() ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="cat_3_py"} `str.contains()` has a `case` argument. Look at what `case=False` does. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="cat_3_py"} ```python is_sub = messy["Description"].str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", case=False) is_sub.sum() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_3_py' check='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: cat_3_py #| check: true if result == 3: feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: all three subscriptions, whatever the capitalization."} else: feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Make the match ignore capitalization."} feedback ``` ::: #### R ::: {.cell exercise='cat_3_r' setup='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_3_r #| setup: true library(dplyr) messy <- data.frame( Description = c("NETFLIX.COM", "Spotify USA", "nytimes digital", "SHELL OIL 1234", "Whole Foods #102"), Amount = c(-15.99, -10.99, -17.00, -45.20, -64.12) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_3_r'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_3_r messy |> filter(grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description)) |> nrow() ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="cat_3_r"} `grepl()` has an `ignore.case` argument. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="cat_3_r"} ```r messy |> filter(grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description, ignore.case = TRUE)) |> nrow() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='cat_3_r' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: cat_3_r #| check: true if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 3))) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: all three subscriptions, whatever the capitalization.") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Make the match ignore capitalization.") } ``` ::: ::: ## Answering Tracking Questions Once every row has a category, the book's three tracking questions take one short pipeline each: what did subscriptions cost, what share of income went to fixed costs, and which variable category was biggest? Spending is stored as negative numbers, so a minus sign turns a spending total positive. ### Level 1: Guided What did the four subscriptions cost this month? ::: panel-tabset #### Excel With `Amount` in `C` and `Category` in `D`, total the subscriptions as a positive number. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution ```swift =-SUMIF(D:D, "Subscriptions", C:C) ``` This returns \$83.97. ::: #### Python ::: {.cell exercise='q_1_py' setup='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: q_1_py #| setup: true import pandas as pd statement = pd.DataFrame({ "Description": [ "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness"], "Amount": [ 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99], "Category": [ "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation", "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions", "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Groceries", "Subscriptions"] }) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='q_1_py'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: q_1_py -statement.loc[statement["Category"] == ______, "Amount"].sum() ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="q_1_py"} Pick the rows whose `Category` is `"Subscriptions"`. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="q_1_py"} ```python -statement.loc[statement["Category"] == "Subscriptions", "Amount"].sum() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='q_1_py' check='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: q_1_py #| check: true if result is not None and abs(result - 83.97) < 0.01: feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $83.97 a month."} else: feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Filter to Subscriptions and keep the minus sign."} feedback ``` ::: #### R ::: {.cell exercise='q_1_r' setup='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: q_1_r #| setup: true library(dplyr) statement <- data.frame( Description = c( "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness"), Amount = c( 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99), Category = c( "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation", "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions", "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Groceries", "Subscriptions") ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='q_1_r'} ```{webr} #| exercise: q_1_r statement |> filter(Category == ______) |> summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |> pull(total) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="q_1_r"} Keep the rows whose `Category` is `"Subscriptions"`. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="q_1_r"} ```r statement |> filter(Category == "Subscriptions") |> summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |> pull(total) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='q_1_r' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: q_1_r #| check: true if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 83.97))) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $83.97 a month.") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Filter to Subscriptions and keep the minus sign.") } ``` ::: ::: ### Level 2: Practice Fixed costs are housing, utilities, and insurance. What share of income went to fixed costs? Give the answer as a decimal (for example, 0.25 for 25%). ::: panel-tabset #### Excel Total the three fixed categories and divide by income (the positive amounts). ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution ```swift =-(SUMIF(D:D,"Housing",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Utilities",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Insurance",C:C))/SUMIF(C:C,">0") ``` This returns 0.803, or about 80%. ::: #### Python ::: {.cell exercise='q_2_py' setup='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: q_2_py #| setup: true import pandas as pd statement = pd.DataFrame({ "Amount": [ 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99], "Category": [ "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation", "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions", "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Groceries", "Subscriptions"] }) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='q_2_py'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: q_2_py fixed = ["Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance"] income = statement.loc[statement["Amount"] > 0, "Amount"].sum() fixed_total = ______ fixed_total / income ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="q_2_py"} `statement["Category"].isin(fixed)` picks the fixed-cost rows. Sum their `Amount` and flip the sign. ::: ::: {.solution exercise="q_2_py"} ```python fixed = ["Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance"] income = statement.loc[statement["Amount"] > 0, "Amount"].sum() fixed_total = -statement.loc[statement["Category"].isin(fixed), "Amount"].sum() fixed_total / income ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='q_2_py' check='true'} ```{pyodide} #| exercise: q_2_py #| check: true if result is not None and abs(result - 0.8030) < 0.001: feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about 80%. This statement has the full month's rent but only one paycheck."} else: feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite.
